images.text: Managing can be challenging, especially when it comes to dealing with people whose personalities clash with your own. I would have preferred beforehand to have the knowledge of how to handle employees while keeping personal feelings separate from work. I would rather have focused on tasks and results than my employee's negative personality traits. Managers shouldn't allow their emotions to interfere, and ought to deal with each employee fairly and without favoritism. However, there are often instances in which managers, such as myself, would sooner ignore an employee I like less than the others than interact with them.
When managers face employees who refuse to do what's asked of them, they ought to make the best of a potentially unpleasant situation by devising a plan that will diffuse the tension.
As a manager, it's high time I confronted problems head-on. Acknowledging any ill will among staff members can help everyone get back to concentrating on the job that needs to be done.
Seek confirmation. When giving instructions, you shouldn't assume you're making yourself clear. If I were you, I would make sure the employee knows what's expected of them.

Rehearse. You should make your requests simple. When you have something complex to say, don't wing it. You should know what you want to say without jumbling words or backtracking. I would rather explain the goal in as few words as possible.

Speak and write. To ensure that employees understand you, you ought to allocate tasks both orally and in print. I would prefer to get into the habit of speaking directly to an employee to tell them what I expect or need. You ought to let the employee make suggestions or ask questions. After you listen carefully to their response, you should  send a follow-up e-mail or memo that reiterates what is expected.

If an employee has an attitude problem, you wouldn't want to allow it to influence or disrupt the job at hand.  Instead, you ought to clarify what tasks need attention. The employee would sooner I avoided making any quips about their track record of not complying with my past requests.

Would Rather, Would Sooner, Would Have Preferred
You use would rather/would sooner + Simple Past or would have preferred to + infinitive to talk about preferences in the present or the future.

You use would rather/would sooner + Simple Past to talk about a preference or strong advice in the present or the future. In this case, you can use it to talk about when you want someone else to do something.
Examples: I'd rather you focused on customer service.
Vanessa would sooner I stayed in the kitchen.

You also use would have preferred to + infinitive to express preference or advice.
Example: I would have preferred to receive higher ratings.

You can use the expression It's high time ... + Past Simple to express a preference about the past or the present.
Example: It's high time we changed our menu.

You use modals like should or ought to to give advice.
You use would with an if-clause to give advice and suggestions about a hypothetical situation.
The most common modals for giving advice are: should, ought to and would.
You can think of modals as “helping verbs”. They add meaning to the main verb of a sentence. In this case, these modals add the meaning of advice.

Should is the most common modal used to give advice.
Ought to is used for giving strong advice.
Would can be used with an if-clause to give personal advice or suggestion as a hypothetical situation, like If I were you, I would ...
